answer.label: Not Sun Tzu — a modern aphorism
answer.authorDates: c. 544 – 496 BC (traditional) · Chinese general & author of The Art of War
answer.sourceLine: This polished strategy-versus-tactics maxim appears in no print translation of Sun Tzu. Wikiquote files it under “Misattributed,” calling it probably apocryphal; its earliest documented sighting in Google Books is only 2002. The strategy/tactics contrast it draws is closer to modern (and Clausewitzian) military vocabulary than to anything in The Art of War.

author.name: Sun Tzu
author.heading: About Sun Tzu
author.metaLine: c. 544 – 496 BC · Chinese general, strategist & author of The Art of War
author.bio: Sun Tzu (Sun Wu) was a Chinese general and military theorist traditionally placed in the late Spring and Autumn period, credited as the author of The Art of War (Sunzi Bingfa), the most influential treatise on strategy ever written. His real text is terse and aphoristic, which is exactly why so many modern, invented one-liners get pinned to his name. The strategy-versus-tactics maxim here is one of them — it does not appear in his work.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution
misattribution.intro: A crisp, quotable line about strategy and tactics, wrapped in Sun Tzu’s name to lend it ancient authority. It is a textbook “magnet-name” fabrication.

items.why: The line appears in no print translation of The Art of War. Wikiquote files it under “Misattributed” as probably apocryphal, with its earliest Google Books trace only in 2002.

The neat “strategy vs. tactics” dichotomy is a modern military-management framing; Sun Tzu’s actual text does not draw the contrast in these terms. This anachronism is our own reading of the line, not a claim documented by any cited source.

misattribution.truthLine: No ancient source: the phrase is a modern aphorism of unknown authorship, attached to Sun Tzu’s name and traceable no earlier than 2002.

context.heading: Why this one spreads
lead: Sun Tzu is one of the internet’s biggest magnets for invented quotes: his real Art of War is short, gnomic and endlessly quotable, so any punchy management-flavored line can be dropped under his name and few readers check. This maxim — balanced, memorable, faintly profound — is perfectly shaped to travel.
The tell is specificity. Genuine Sun Tzu quotations can be pinned to a chapter and a translator (Giles, Griffith, and others). This one never is, because there is nothing to pin it to.
context.pull: Real Sun Tzu comes with a chapter and a translator. This line comes with neither.
